title.en: The Kuinasarinook: Uvnek Summons the Amarsiniook
title.zh: 庫伊納薩里努克：烏夫內克召喚山魔

region.en: Firth of Godthaab and the monster-mountains

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 116 'The Kuinasarinook', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Uvnek, one of the last angakut at the firth of Godthaab, on one of his spirit-flights narrowly escaped being taken by an amarsiniook; after his return he once performed a conjuration and summoned the amarsiniook — a brightness was observed, and a voice from above the house: 'If thou hadst not happened to be an angakok thou wouldst never have escaped; it was I who killed the kuinasarinook (another monster dwelling in certain mountains), because it had torn a man to pieces.' The auditors remembered how some time ago a man had been found dead, his body terribly mutilated, nobody able to make out how the murder was committed till it was thus explained by Uvnek.
summary.zh: 努克峽灣末代巫師之一的烏夫內克，在一次靈魂飛行中險遭山魔阿馬爾西尼奧克擄走；歸來後他降神召其現身——屋頂上方亮光一閃，傳來聲音：『若你不是巫師，斷難逃脫。是我殺了庫伊納薩里努克（另一種居於某些山中的魔怪），因為它把一個人撕成了碎片。』眾人這才想起：先前確有一人陳屍荒野、殘缺難辨，兇手成謎——直到烏夫內克一語道破。

passages.text: Uvnek, one of the last angakut at the firth of Godthaab, on one of his spirit-flights narrowly escaped being taken by an amarsiniook. After his return he once performed a conjuration and summoned the amarsiniook — a brightness was observed, and a voice was heard from above the house saying, 'If thou hadst not happened to be an angakok thou wouldst never have escaped; it was I who killed the kuinasarinook (another monster, dwelling in certain mountains), because it had torn a man to pieces.' The auditors then remembered how some time ago a man had been found dead and his body terribly mutilated; but nobody had been able to make out how the murder was committed till it was thus explained by Uvnek.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 116 'The Kuinasarinook'; not verbatim.

title.en: Ajagutarsuk and Ularpana: The Tornaks' Duel
title.zh: 阿亞古塔舒克與烏拉爾帕納：靈助對決

region.en: The cave and the dried-up lake

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 117 'An Old Man who was always anxious to outdo other People', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two old men anxious to outdo everyone bet in turn on whose wife should first get a son, then which son should become the greatest angakok: Ajagutarsuk attained angakok wisdom in a cave, Ularpana acquired it in a dried-up lake. The latter flew to visit the former, who called forth his tornaks belonging to the inlanders — but Ularpana invoked his, the upper ingnersuit, who totally defeated the inlanders.
summary.zh: 兩位事事爭勝的老人先賭誰的妻子先得子，再賭誰的兒子能成為最偉大的巫師：阿亞古塔舒克在巖穴中修得巫智，烏拉爾帕納在乾涸的湖底得道。後者飛往探望前者——阿亞古塔舒克召出內陸人的靈助；烏拉爾帕納則喚出上位因格內爾舒特人，把內陸人殺得大敗。

passages.text: An Old Man who was always anxious to outdo other People had laid a bet with his friend as to whose wife should first get a son, and afterwards as to which of their sons should in course of time become the greatest angakok. One of them, Ajagutarsuk, attained angakok wisdom in a cave; and the other, named Ularpana, acquired it in a dried-up lake. The latter went on an angakok flight to the first, and while staying with him Ajagutarsuk called forth his tornaks which belonged to the inlanders, and instantly appeared — but Ularpana invoked his tornaks, being the upper ingnersuit, who totally defeated the inlanders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 117 'An Old Man who was always anxious to outdo other People'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Revenging Animals: The Merganser's Eggs
title.zh: 復仇的動物：秋沙鴨之卵

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 118 'The Revenging Animals', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A great angakok seized by a longing for eggs carries off a merganser's whole nest — and on the way home the robbed seals voice their plan: fetch a piece of ice and return as umiarissat. The filth thrown on the beach turns their seal-manned boat to a piece of ice; later the gooseander's head emerges from the entrance with dreadfully enlarged eyes — come to fetch its eggs back by a charm that made him forget them in his kayak; had he not left them it certainly would have frightened them all to death. Another angakok in a similar case was bereft of his angakok power by the merganser.
summary.zh: 貪食鳥蛋的大巫師搬空了秋沙鴨的整巢——歸途上被搶的海豹群商議：『去搬塊冰來，化作幽靈之舟報仇！』灘上潑灑的穢物令那艘海豹駕驭的大舟現出冰塊原形；入夜，鵲鴨之頭自門口探出、雙眼脹得駭人——它是來討回鳥蛋的，靠咒術使他忘了蛋還在艇上；若非他恰好忘帶，必把全屋的人嚇死。另一位犯下同樣過錯的巫師，則被秋沙鴨奪去了全部法力。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; umiarissat = the avenging boat-people of overkilled seals (compare tale 14 note).

passages.text: A great angakok, while kayaking about at midsummer, suddenly took a longing for eggs; landing upon an island he found a merganser's nest with plenty of eggs, all of which he carried away. On his way home he met with a flock of seals of which he harpooned one — but after having taken it he heard voices from among the rest encouraging each other to go and get hold of a piece of ice and return as umiarissat. On getting home he walked up to his house forgetting the eggs in his kayak, but ordered his housemates to throw down on the beach all manner of filthy stuff to frighten away the umiarissat — in the evening a boat was seen to arrive manned with seals, but as soon as they scented the filth they all jumped into the water and the boat appeared as a piece of ice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 118 'The Revenging Animals'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Later in the evening a voice was heard outside, and the head of the gooseander emerged from the entrance with dreadfully enlarged eyes; addressing itself to the angakok it scolded him for having robbed it of its descendants, but now it had come to fetch its eggs back, having by help of a charm caused him to forget them and leave them in his kayak — if he had not left them it certainly would have frightened them all to death. Another angakok in a similar case was bereft of his angakok power by the merganser.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 118 'The Revenging Animals'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Igdlokok: The Guest with One Footprint
title.zh: 伊格德洛洛克：只留一隻腳印的客人

region.en: Lonely house of the mourning man

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 119 'The Igdlokok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Having seen his beloved cousin torn to pieces by a sorcery-made bear, a man braves every danger for excitement and first kills an amarok — then a talkative stranger drops into his lonely house, also mourning a brother, and spends the evening pleasantly until the hostess serves the boiled amarok-flesh: 'But I see the dish is all aslope' — and the same instant he vanishes through the entrance. His footsteps in the snow are made by only one foot: the guest must have been an igdlokok, whose body is only the one half of the human body cut in twain.
summary.zh: 親眼目睹摯友被術造之熊撕碎的男子，為求刺激而歷險，先殺一頭狼靈阿馬洛克；夜裡一名健談的陌生人不請自入——同樣是喪失兄弟而四處歷險的人——賓主盡歡，直到女主人端上燉好的狼靈肉。客人連聲稱贊其香其色，卻忽然說：『可惜這盤子是斜的。』話音未落便穿門而去。雪地上的腳印只有一隻——原來那是伊格德洛洛克：軀體只有人被剖開的一半。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; note records a variant where the vanishing guests appear as the stars Siagtut or Qilugtussat.

passages.text: A man had lost his beloved cousin and friend, who in his sight had been torn to pieces by one of those bears that are made by sorcery. In his despair he went out to encounter and brave all kinds of danger by way of excitement, and first killed an amarok. One evening when staying at home he was surprised in his lonely house by a stranger dropping in, who explained that he also having lost his brother was roaming about for excitement; being very talkative he spent the evening there very pleasantly, until the hostess who had boiled some flesh of the amarok came and served it before the men. The guest then burst out in loud praises of its delicious flavour and tempting appearance — but before he had taken a morsel he went on, 'But I see the dish is all aslope,' and the same instant arose and vanished through the entrance. The host immediately followed him; and on examining his footsteps in the snow found them to be made by only one foot, so that the guest must have been an igdlokok (whose body is only the one half of the human body cut in twain).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 119 'The Igdlokok'; not verbatim.

title.en: Iviangersook Travelled All Around the Coast of Greenland
title.zh: 伊萬格舒克環格陵蘭海岸記

region.en: Cape Farewell, the eastward light-haired people, and Ilulissat Sound
region.zh: 費爾韋爾角、東岸淺髮族人與伊盧利薩特水道

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 120 'Iviangersook travelled all around the Coast of Greenland', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Starting for the south and passing Cape Farewell, Iviangersook came on the eastward to some light-haired people of European complexion, and lastly returned through the Sound, which was formerly open from east to west, near Ilulissat (Jakobshavn). When approaching his home near Godthaab he lost his brother, who was buried upon a small island after them named Uviarniak — one who travelled all around.
summary.zh: 伊萬格舒克南行繞過費爾韋爾角，在東岸遇見淺色頭髮、面貌如歐人的部族；最後經由昔日貫通東西的水道——伊盧利薩特附近——返航。將抵努克家園時失去了兄弟；他被葬在一座小島上，島從此以他們命名為烏維亞尼亞克——『環行一周者』。

passages.text: Iviangersook travelled all around the Coast of Greenland: he started for the south, and having passed Cape Farewell came on the eastward to some light-haired people of European complexion, and lastly returned through the Sound which was formerly open from east to west near Ilulissat (Jakobshavn). When approaching his home near Godthaab he lost his brother, who was buried upon a small island after them named Uviarniak (one who travelled all around).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 120 'Iviangersook travelled all around the Coast of Greenland'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Childless Couple Who Were Both Angakok

region.en: Foreign place with the witch's ghost

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 121 'A Married Couple remained childless on account of their both being Angakok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Kayaking together as always, the angakok couple finds a young man almost dying in a foreign place; the man conjures the witch, detects her ghost approaching to touch the youth with her black hands, thrusts his harpoon at her heel — and almost at the same moment the aunt dies in the next house, proved to have been the witch. Envying the playing children — 'That crowd of boys might almost make people envious' — they are answered: 'The boys yonder are the namesakes of those whom the monster-gulls carried off as food for their young ones' — and the whole assembly at once becomes silent.
summary.zh: 相偕出海的巫師夫婦在異鄉遇見一名垂死的青年；丈夫降神召出害人的巫婆——識得她的鬼魂正要以黑手觸碰病者——一叉刺中她的腳跟；幾乎同時，隔壁的姑母死了，正是那巫婆。羨慕屋中嬉戲的孩子——『這群男孩簡直叫人嫉妒』——得到的回答是：『他們都是被巨鷗抓去餵雛的那些人的承名者』（即葬身海上者）——滿屋霎時寂然。

passages.text: The husband and wife always used to go out kayaking together; once they happened to come to a foreign place where a young man was found in an almost dying state. The angakok-man began a conjuration summoning the witch who had caused his sickness — he detected the ghost of the witch approaching the sick youth in order to touch him with her black hands, but the angakok thrust his harpoon at her, hitting her heel; almost at the same moment the aunt of the sick youth died in the next house and proved to have been the witch. While spending the rest of the evening there eating and talking in a pleasant way the visitors noticed the children playing on the floor; and thinking of their own childless state burst out, 'That crowd of boys might almost make people envious' — they were answered, 'The boys yonder are the namesakes of those whom the monster-gulls carried off as food for their young ones' (viz., who perished in kayaks); whereupon the whole assembly at once became silent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 121 'A Married Couple remained childless on account of their both being Angakok'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Man Who Killed the Inlander Using the Fog as Kayak
title.zh: 以霧為艇：老人誤殺內陸人

region.en: The son's grave up the firth

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 122 'An Old Man lost his only Son', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Visiting his son's reindeer-hunting grave, an old man sees an inlander pulling himself through the water without any kayak — 'using the fog as kayak' — and after some angry words kills him. Another time an inlander questions his grief — 'Yonder wretched heap of stones is the only object of my distress' — and tells how he also lost a son seal-hunting: the old man makes out it must have been the one he had killed, pretends to be expected home, pushes off in his skiff, and never more visits the grave of his son.
summary.zh: 常去峽灣深處兒子墳前憑弔的老人，一日見一名內陸人不駕艇而自行划水而來——『以霧為艇』——爭執幾句後將其殺死。再訪墳塋時，另一名內陸人問他何以悲傷——『那一堆可憐的石頭便是我全部的哀愁』——並說自己也折了一個出海的兒子；老人認出那正是被他殺死的年輕人，謊稱家人等他回去，掉槳而去，從此再不上墳。

passages.text: An Old Man lost his only Son when they were both reindeer-hunting up the country; after returning home he often used to visit his son's grave. Kayaking up the firth with this view he once right before him saw an inlander pulling himself through the water without any kayak ('using the fog as kayak'), and after some angry words killed the inlander. Another time when he was again visiting the grave he was surprised at the sight of an inlander who questioned him as to the cause of his grief — 'Yonder wretched heap of stones is the only object of my distress,' he answered. The inlander then told him how he also had some time ago lost a son who had been seal-hunting; the old man made out that it must have been the one he had killed — on which he pretended to be expected home, pushed off in his skiff, and never more visited the grave of his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 122 'An Old Man lost his only Son'; not verbatim.

title.en: Angakorsiak: Shame Turned Him into a Reindeer

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 123 'Angakorsiak was very proud of his Angakok Wisdom', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Proud of his angakok wisdom, Angakorsiak challenges a northern rival in broad daylight: he cuts off his arm near the shoulder, replaces it drinking the blood, swallows an arrow-point and makes it appear again, opens his stomach with a knife — the rival repeats all with the utmost perfection and proposes a kayak-race, casting a harpoon into a rock so it enters the stone and blood springs from it. Angakorsiak fails, harpoon broken and lost, capsizes from shame and sinks — a reindeer immediately emerges and runs up the beach; shame having thus transformed him, he turns man again and hastens away, resolved to give up all kind of emulation in future.
summary.zh: 自負巫智的安加科夏克向北方同行下戰書：當眾斬臂、接臂飲血、吞箭吐箭、剖腹示腸——對手分毫不差地重演一遍，還提議賽艇：一叉擲入巖石，入石三分、石上迸血。安加科夏克如法炮製卻叉斷柄折；歸途羞愧低頭、翻艇沉底——轉瞬一頭馴鹿出水奔上山坡：羞愧把他變成了鹿。他復為人形後倉皇而去，發誓從此不再與人爭勝。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; several variants exist of the angakut's deeds.

passages.text: Angakorsiak was very proud of his Angakok Wisdom, and always roamed about seeking opportunities of emulating other angakut; when he happened to surpass them he used to mock and ridicule them in a most overbearing manner. Once he visited an angakok far up north and challenged him to a match, at which, in broad daylight, they were to contend in working the wonders of their art before an assembly. Angakorsiak began his performance by cutting off his arm near the shoulder, inserting it again and drinking the blood from the wound; after which he swallowed an arrow-point and made it appear again, opened his stomach with a knife, and so on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 123 'Angakorsiak was very proud of his Angakok Wisdom'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When he had finished the other angakok repeated the same feats with the utmost perfection, and then remarked, 'Well, what we have yet done amounts to nothing; but I should now like to try a kayak-race with thee.' They went down in their kayaks, and the angakok of the place taking his way to an island threw his harpoon at a rock with such force as to make it enter the stone and blood to spring from it — Angakorsiak on trying this entirely failed, his harpoon being broken and lost. On their way back to the shore he bent down his head from shame, capsized his kayak, and sank — but directly afterwards a reindeer emerged from the water and ran up on the beach. Shame having thus transformed him into a reindeer he afterwards turned a man again, and hastened away, resolved to give up all kind of emulation in future.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 123 'Angakorsiak was very proud of his Angakok Wisdom'; not verbatim.

title.en: Tuagtuanguak: Five Days at the Precipice
title.zh: 圖阿格圖安瓜克：懸崖五日

region.en: The northern flight-road and the ingnersuit country
region.zh: 北行之路與因格內爾舒特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 124 'A Girl named Tuagtuanguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Fleeing her persecuting brother-in-law across the ice, Tuagtuanguak falls through, gets up, and runs on north viewing a black spot before her — swooning several times, acquiring angakok power between swoons, five successive days to a precipice whose leap wafts her back through the air for five days more. Settling and marrying in the north, she visits the ingnersuit and receives presents — but carrying them homewards the gifts are wafted out of her hands and fly back to their first owners.
summary.zh: 為逃避姑丈糾纏而踏冰奔逃的圖阿格圖安瓜克落入冰縫又爬起，一路向北追著眼前的黑點——幾度昏厥，昏醒之間漸得巫力；連行五日至絕崖，躍而過之，卻被一股氣流送回原處，如是者五日。北地安家成婚後，她往訪因格內爾舒特人並受贈禮——然而攜禮歸途，禮物竟脫手飛回原主。

passages.text: A Girl named Tuagtuanguak fled from her brother-in-law who persecuted her; running across the ice she fell through, but having again got up she ran on and on to the north constantly viewing a black spot before her. Swooning several times and again seeing the black spot on awaking she meanwhile acquired angakok power; going on in this way for five successive days she came to a precipice, and setting out from its edge leaped across — but was somehow wafted back through the air to the same spot; this process she continued for five days. She then pursued her journey north and came to an inhabited place where she took up her abode and afterwards got married. She visited the ingnersuit and received presents from them — but while carrying them homewards the gifts were wafted out of her hands and flew back to their first owners.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 124 'A Girl named Tuagtuanguak'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Gifts from the Under-World: The Two Boats

region.en: The stone-covered entrance to the under-world

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 125 'The Gifts from the Under-world', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Envious of a younger man's luck and favour with women, an old bachelor is sent by his mother to a large stone: moving it aside, an opening leads straight to the under-world and a lake with two boats — let the first pass, apply to the second. Eating the matak from the second boat gives him astonishing luck; the young man, coached with the first boat substituted, secures only the worst luck in his hunting — and the old man, returning for more, finds himself quite unable to move the stone.
summary.zh: 嫉妒年輕人獵運亨通、深受女子青睞的老鰥夫，依母親指點挪開巨石，循孔道直下冥界之湖：兩舟並至，讓頭舟過，向次舟求取——吞下那片鯨皮，獵運驚人。年輕人追問法門，老鰥夫故意把『頭舟』『次舟』對調相告——年輕人求得的卻是最壞的運氣；老鰥夫食畢再去，巨石卻再也搬不動了。

passages.text: An old bachelor, feeling envious of a younger one because of his better luck in hunting and his finding more favour with women, applied to his mother for counsel and aid. She pointed out to him a certain spot where he would find a large stone, and moving it aside an opening would appear leading straight to the under-world, where he would come to a lake; and on seeing two boats he was to let the first one pass but was to apply to the second.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 125 'The Gifts from the Under-world'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Acting upon her advice he received a piece of matak (whale-skin) from the second boat, by eating which he acquired astonishing good-luck in hunting; the young man noticing this change of fortune questioned him as to the cause of his recent success, when he imparted to him the information he had gained from his mother only substituting the first boat for the second — the young man in this way also got a piece of matak, by eating which he only secured the worst luck in his hunting. Meanwhile the old man had consumed his piece and went to fetch more; but when he came to the spot the second time he found himself quite unable to move the stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 125 'The Gifts from the Under-world'; not verbatim.
